newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle lands in Florida.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle lands in Florida.

text.p: The space shuttle Atlantis landed in Florida on Wednesday, ending a 54-million-mile (68.4 million km) orbital odyssey for astronaut John Blaha.
The $2 billion reusable spaceship glided through blue skies to touch down at NASA's Kennedy Space Centre at 9:22 a.m. EST (1422 GMT).
"Welcome back after a super mission," mission control's Kevin Kregel said. "And a special welcome back to John after his four months on Mir."
"It feels great to be back," replied the veteran astronaut.

The shuttle was returning from its fifth visit to the Russian space station, where it had picked up Blaha and dropped off his replacement, Jerry Linenger. Its homecoming had been delayed for 90 minutes because of clouds at the Florida spaceport, but the sky cleared in time for Atlantis' second landing opportunity.
Blaha's 128 days in space was the second-longest mission by an American. Astronaut Shannon Lucid set the record of 188 days during a flight to Mir last year.

The 54-year-old Blaha rode back to Earth on the shuttle's mid-deck in a cushioned reclining seat, his chest wired with medical sensors so doctors could monitor his health as gravity gripped his body for the first time in four months.
Officials were uncertain how quickly he would readapt to Earth's pull. The two previous U.S. Mir occupants were able to walk from the shuttle cabin.
Two NASA doctors entered Atlantis soon after landing to examine Blaha before he attempted to leave. A stretcher was available if he was unable to stand.
He was expected to be reunited at the runway with Brenda, his wife of 30 years. He said he had missed her more than anything else during his time aboard the isolated outpost.

Atlantis had blasted off from the Kennedy Space Centre 10 days earlier and arrived at Mir on Jan. 14 to cheers from Blaha and his two Russian crewmates. In addition to exchanging U.S. crewmembers, the shuttle delivered more than three tonnes of supplies and equipment to the 11-year-old space station.
The cash-strapped Russian space agency now relies on the shuttle to deliver about 40 percent of the station's supplies.

Atlantis departed Mir on Sunday, leaving Linenger to perform more than 80 scientific experiments and make the first space walk from Mir by an American. The shuttle was to return to the Russian station in May to bring Linenger's replacement.
Meanwhile, five miles (8 km) west of the runway, shuttle Discovery was being prepared at the launch pad for a February mission to refurbish and repair the Hubble Space Telescope.
